extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying patent litigation procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing jurisdiction, parties, service, and standing in actions for patent infringement (both law and equity), as explained in a treatise on the law of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive federal jurisdiction over patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction over all cases arising under the Patent Laws is vested exclusively in the Federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions for infringement, whether at law or in equity, must be instituted in one of the Circuit courts of the United States or equivalent tribunals (District and Territorial courts with circuit powers, Supreme Court of D.C.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality determines which Circuit court should hear a case
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining what particular Circuit court has jurisdiction of any individual case, the question of locality is of paramount importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action for damages for past infringements is not a local action and any competent court may hear it; nevertheless the particular court should be the one whose local jurisdiction embraces the parties to the suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between actions at law and in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions at law and actions in equity differ in procedure and in the rules for determining compensation; equity jurisdiction may require more direct and permanent control over parties/subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular Circuit court may decline equitable proceedings that it would entertain at law if the enforcement demands broader control; injunctions warrant separate examination because of their complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for actions at law — where defendant resides or is found
rubrics_metrics.description: An action at law for infringement may be brought before any Circuit court which has jurisdiction over the persons of the plaintiff and defendant; a defendant is within jurisdiction when he resides or is lawfully served with process in the district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff places himself in the court by instituting action there. For non-residents, personal service within the circuit is required; service by publication or attachment does not satisfy Federal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction venue rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be issued against an infringer in the district where he resides, does business, or where the infringement takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cited cases (e.g., Hatch v. Hall, Wilson Packing Co. v. Glapp) establishing these venue bases for injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal service requirement for non-residents
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal service within the circuit must be made upon a non-resident defendant and must affirmatively appear on the marshal's return or the court acquires no jurisdiction over him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service must be lawful and not procured by fraud or imposition; service obtained by inveigling the defendant into the circuit is fraudulent and void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service obtained by fraud is void
rubrics_metrics.description: Service on a non-resident who was inveigled or fraudulently brought within the circuit for the purpose of service is fraudulent and void and will be set aside on motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if improper service occurred, the defendant may appear and submit to jurisdiction, after which the court's authority is as complete as if regular service had been obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance and waiver rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A party appearing submits to the jurisdiction; irregularities in service are waived unless objected to before answer. An appearance solely to move to quash or plead to jurisdiction does not waive such objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry of a special appearance to challenge jurisdiction does not necessarily waive defects; but general appearance or pleading to jurisdiction admits and submits to the court's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marshal's return must affirmatively show lawful service
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person is sued out of his own district, it must affirmatively appear by the marshal's return that process was served on him in the district where the suit is brought, or the court will acquire no jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to show proper service in the return can defeat jurisdiction (cases cited: Thayer v. Wales, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service while attending court or at stipulated examinations is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Service upon a defendant attending court in another State as a party defendant, or attending by stipulation for witness examinations, is not lawful and will be set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service on such occasions has been held void (e.g., Wilson Sewing Mach. Co. v. Wilson; Plimpton v. Winslow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation location and service — where organized
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation organized under the laws of a State is located at all places within the limits of that State and may be sued in any Circuit court whose jurisdiction embraces any portion of such State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service upon officers of a non-resident corporation outside its State is ineffective; whether a corporation can be served outside its State of creation is doubtful unless local law provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Found" within a State for service of process
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign corporation doing business in a State is 'found within the State' for purposes of suit if it can be served with process there under State laws, especially where the State appoints resident officials for service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owning property or merely sending agents to purchase raw materials is not necessarily being 'found'; establishing an office or agency for carrying on the business for which it was incorporated typically suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing agent suffices for service
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'managing agent' — one who carries on corporate business or a substantial part thereof — may be treated as a person 'found' within the district so that service on him is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The managing agent need not control the corporation's entire business; New York and other courts have recognized service on managing agents as valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation sued where it does business via appointed agents
rubrics_metrics.description: If State laws provide that foreign corporations doing business in the State appoint resident officials upon whom service may be made, such corporations are 'found' within that State for jurisdictional purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates amenability to suit in local and Federal courts for actions arising from corporate activity in the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit courts that embrace multiple districts treat districts as local units
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Circuit court or its equivalent tribunal has jurisdiction over two or more districts, each district becomes the local unit of jurisdiction; a defendant must be sued in his own district or a district where he can be lawfully served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If joint defendants live in different districts, proceedings may be commenced in either; corporate location rules follow whether a State equals a single district or is subdivided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff in law must be legal owner at date of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff in an action at law must be the person(s) in whom the legal title to the patent resided at the time of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the patentee, his assignee, grantee, or personal representatives can maintain a legal action for infringement; the injury falls upon the individual owning the monopoly at the infringement date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignees and joinder necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignees are indispensable parties in infringement suits; parties equitably interested need not be joined as plaintiffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an assignment transfers title for the whole term (as a transfer, not merely a license), the assignee is the proper plaintiff in equity; assignments coupled with rights of action for past infringements may transfer rights to sue for past infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensees cannot sue in their own name at law
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee of a patent cannot bring a suit in his own name, at law or in equity, for its infringement by a stranger; an action for the licensee's benefit must be brought in the name of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite exclusive territorial or use rights, a licensee is only a licensee; suits at law for redress of infringements affecting a licensee must generally be brought in the patentee's name. However, if the patentee refuses or is inaccessible, the licensee may in some circumstances sue for damages in his own name (text discusses this exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of relief available to licensees versus owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensees and holders of equitable interests are debarred from suing for infringement in their own names in courts of law; equity may offer different relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee may be protected by a guaranty from the licensor; where the legal owner refuses or is inaccessible, equitable remedies or suits in the patentee's name may be pursued to protect the licensee's practical rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular service and waiver rules for corporations and agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Service on one co-partner does not give personal jurisdiction over a non-resident partner; service cannot be made on an agent created by implication against the will of parties; irregularities are waived unless objected to before answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearance by attorney and plea to jurisdiction admits and submits to jurisdiction; service on an agent or officer outside the State of corporate creation does not acquire jurisdiction over the corporation.
